# Module 15: Native Library Interoperability

::: notes
This module shows how to reuse a mature HPC library without exposing its raw
pointer API to the rest of the application. Keep the focus on boundary
invariants, not on Fourier-transform theory.
:::

## Module Arc

- Start with a signal whose spectrum is predictable
- Identify what the C API cannot express to Rust
- Own native buffers and plans with Rust types
- Concentrate `unsafe` behind slice-based methods
- Compare the local wrapper with the high-level `fftw` crate
- Build the full binding stack for a home-grown C++ library
- Export optional visualization data through typed CLI paths
- Validate both boundary failures and scientific behavior

::: notes
Connect this to the OpenBLAS-backed SVD example: there learners consumed a safe
wrapper. Here they first build one around FFTW's raw bindings, then replace
that boundary code with an existing safe crate.
:::

## A Testable Signal

```text
x[j] =
    sin(2 pi 3 j / n)
    + 0.5 cos(2 pi 7 j / n)
```

- 64 real samples
- Expected dominant bins: 3 and 7
- Forward transform, inverse transform, error check
- Optional signal and power-spectrum CSV

::: notes
Ask for the expected bins before showing any Rust. This makes the later test a
scientific property rather than a check that the FFI call did not crash.
:::

## Four Layers

```text
main.rs
  safe vectors and Result
          |
RealFft
  safe slice-based wrapper
          |
fftw-sys
  raw pointers and unsafe calls
          |
libfftw3.so
```

::: notes
The sys crate supplies declarations close to C. RealFft is the abstraction
boundary owned by this project.
:::

::: notes
On an HPC system, replace the package-manager command with the site's FFTW

## What Rust Cannot Check

- Does the pointer reference enough elements?
- Is the allocation aligned as FFTW requires?
- Is the complex buffer exactly `n / 2 + 1` elements?
- Does the plan outlive its buffers?
- Which planner operations require serialization?
- Which native function releases each resource?

::: notes
Unsafe does not disable these requirements. It tells the compiler that this
block is relying on facts established elsewhere.
:::

## Validate Before FFI

```rust
if length == 0 {
    return Err(FftError::EmptyInput);
}

let ffi_length = i32::try_from(length)
    .map_err(|_| FftError::LengthTooLarge(length))?;
```

- Rust API: `usize`
- C API: `int`
- Conversion failure becomes a normal error

::: notes
Also show the slice-length checks in real_fft.rs. The native call should never
be responsible for discovering an undersized Rust slice.
:::

## Own Aligned Memory

```rust
struct FftwBuffer<T> {
    pointer: NonNull<T>,
    length: usize,
}
```

- FFTW performs the allocation
- `NonNull` records successful construction
- Length travels with the pointer
- Memory is initialized before creating Rust slices

::: notes
Open source-code/fftw-ffi/src/real_fft.rs for the allocation calls and their
safety comments. Do not place the full implementation on the slide.
:::

## Release With `Drop`

```rust
impl<T> Drop for FftwBuffer<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        unsafe {
            fftw_free(self.pointer.as_ptr().cast());
        }
    }
}
```

- FFTW allocation pairs with FFTW deallocation
- Early `?` returns still clean up constructed values
- Native ownership becomes Rust RAII

::: notes
Plans have a matching Drop implementation using fftw_destroy_plan. Contrast
this with manually repeating cleanup at every return site.
:::

## Drop Order Is An Invariant

```rust
pub struct RealFft {
    length: usize,
    spectrum_length: usize,
    forward_plan: FftwPlan,
    inverse_plan: FftwPlan,
    real_buffer: FftwBuffer<f64>,
    complex_buffer: FftwBuffer<Complex64>,
}
```

- Plans retain buffer addresses
- Fields drop in declaration order
- Plans are destroyed before buffers

::: notes
Moving RealFft is still valid because its FFTW allocations remain at stable
heap addresses.
:::

## Preserve Native Concurrency Rules

```rust
static FFTW_PLANNER_LOCK: Mutex<()> = Mutex::new(());

fn lock_planner() -> MutexGuard<'static, ()> {
    FFTW_PLANNER_LOCK
        .lock()
        .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner)
}
```

- Plan creation and destruction are serialized
- Independent plan execution remains unlocked

::: notes
A wrapper that works only when constructed on one thread is not yet a sound
general-purpose safe API. Encode the library's actual concurrency rule.
:::

## Real Transform Shape

```text
real input:      n
complex output:  floor(n / 2) + 1

n = 64  ->  33 complex values
```

```rust
let spectrum_length = length / 2 + 1;
```

- Real input has a conjugate-symmetric spectrum
- FFTW returns only the non-redundant half

::: notes
This is both a numerical fact and a buffer-allocation invariant at the FFI
boundary.
:::

## One-Sided Mean-Square Power

```text
P[k] = c[k] |X[k]|^2 / n^2

c[k] = 1  at DC and Nyquist
c[k] = 2  otherwise
```

```text
sum(P[k]) = sum(x[j]^2) / n
```

- Bin 3: `0.5`
- Bin 7: `0.125`
- Total: `0.625`

::: notes
The factor of two accounts for the omitted negative-frequency partner. The
Nyquist bin exists only for even signal lengths and must not be doubled.
:::

## Normalize The Inverse

```rust
let normalization = self.length as f64;

let reconstructed = self
    .real_buffer
    .as_slice()
    .iter()
    .map(|value| value / normalization)
    .collect();
```

- FFTW's inverse is unnormalized
- The inverse may overwrite its complex input
- Copy into owned native storage before execution

::: notes
Remove the division during a live edit and ask participants to predict the
scale of the reconstructed signal.
:::

## The Public API Is Safe

```rust
let mut transform = RealFft::new(signal.len())?;

let spectrum = transform.forward(&signal)?;
let reconstructed = transform.inverse(&spectrum)?;
```

- No public raw pointers
- No returned borrow into reusable FFTW storage
- Length failures use `FftError`
- Native failures propagate through `Result`

::: notes
Returning owned vectors is a deliberate teaching choice. A borrowed zero-copy
result would need a more restrictive API because the next transform overwrites
the internal buffer.
:::

## Use The Existing `fftw` Crate

```toml
fftw = {
    version = "0.8.0",
    default-features = false,
    features = ["system"]
}
```

```rust
let mut input = AlignedVec::new(length);
input.copy_from_slice(signal);

let mut spectrum = AlignedVec::new(length / 2 + 1);
let mut plan = R2CPlan64::aligned(
    &[length],
    Flag::ESTIMATE,
)?;
plan.r2c(&mut input, &mut spectrum)?;
```

::: notes
The safe crate still uses fftw-sys internally. It moves responsibility for
aligned allocation, plan ownership, raw calls, and native errors out of the
application.
:::

## What The Safe Crate Removes

| Local `fftw-sys` wrapper | Application using `fftw` |
|---|---|
| `NonNull` and allocation wrappers | `AlignedVec` |
| Local plan and `Drop` types | Owning plan types |
| Raw pointer calls | Safe transform methods |
| Local planner lock | Crate-managed planning |
| Safety comments and invariants | No application `unsafe` |

Still application responsibilities:

- Inverse normalization
- One-sided power definition
- CLI and output schemas
- Scientific tests

::: notes
Both projects solve the same numerical problem and generate byte-identical CSV
files. The raw version teaches how safety is established; the high-level
version shows what application code should normally prefer when the API fits.
:::

## When No Binding Crate Exists

`source-code/cpp-interpolation-ffi`

```text
safe Rust API
      |
raw Rust declarations
      |
stable extern "C" facade
      |
C++ LinearInterpolator
```

- Home-grown C++ source is part of the project
- No `-sys` crate supplies declarations or linking
- The project owns every boundary layer

::: notes
This is the practical motivation for writing a complete binding. FFTW is still
the richer scientific example, but normal applications should use its existing
safe crate. The interpolation project models the common in-house-library case.
:::

## Give The C++ Class A C ABI

```c
typedef struct interpolation_handle interpolation_handle;

int interpolation_create(
    const double* x, size_t x_len,
    const double* y, size_t y_len,
    interpolation_handle** output
);

int interpolation_evaluate(
    const interpolation_handle* handle,
    double x, double* output
);
```

- Opaque handle hides the C++ class layout
- Pointer-length pairs describe borrowed arrays
- Status codes cross the ABI; exceptions do not

::: notes
The C facade catches every C++ exception. Construction copies the arrays, so
the resulting object does not retain pointers into Rust slices.
:::

## Build And Declare The Boundary

```rust
// build.rs
cc::Build::new()
    .cpp(true)
    .std("c++17")
    .file("native/interpolator.cpp")
    .file("native/interpolator_c.cpp")
    .compile("interpolation");
```

```rust
unsafe extern "C" {
    fn interpolation_destroy(
        handle: *mut InterpolationHandle,
    );
}
```

::: notes
The cc crate selects the native compiler and emits Cargo link instructions.
The handwritten declaration is manageable because the C API is deliberately
small; discuss bindgen as the scalable alternative for larger headers.
:::

## Recover Rust Ownership And Errors

```rust
pub struct LinearInterpolator {
    handle: NonNull<InterpolationHandle>,
    minimum: f64,
    maximum: f64,
}

impl Drop for LinearInterpolator {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        unsafe {
            interpolation_destroy(self.handle.as_ptr())
        };
    }
}
```

- Safe methods accept slices and return `Result`
- Status codes become `InterpolationError` variants
- `Drop` releases the C++ object exactly once

::: notes
Trace ownership upward: C++ allocation, opaque C handle, non-null pointer, and
owning Rust value. Unsafe stays in the raw call and cleanup implementation.
:::

```{.bash}
cargo run -- --query 1.5
cargo run -- --query 5.0
cargo test
```

```text
Interpolated value at x = 1.5: 2.5
```

- Included C++ source; no native package installation
- Boundary and numerical tests

::: notes
Use the failing query to trace one status code from C++ through the C facade
into the Rust error enum. A C++ compiler is the only native prerequisite.
:::

## Scientific `-sys` And Wrapper Crates

| Native library | Raw bindings | Wrapper |
|---|---|---|
| FFTW | `fftw-sys` | `fftw` |
| MPI | `mpi-sys` | `mpi` |
| HDF5 | `hdf5-metno-sys` | `hdf5-metno` |
| netCDF | `netcdf-sys` | `netcdf` |
| SUNDIALS | `sundials-sys` | `sundials` |
| BLAS | `blas-sys` | `blas` |
| LAPACK | `lapack-sys` | `lapack`, `ndarray-linalg` |

- Coverage and safety level differ between wrappers
- `blas` and `lapack` calls remain `unsafe`
- `ndarray-linalg` provides higher-level array methods

::: notes
Treat this as a discovery map, not an endorsement. A project still needs to
check native-version coverage, maintenance, thread safety, error handling, and
system-linking behavior. Connect ndarray-linalg back to the SVD example and
`hdf5-metno` to `source-code/hdf5-snapshot`; that project renames the package
to `hdf5` for concise source paths.
:::

## Optional Visualization Output

```{.bash}
cargo run -- \
  --signal-output signal.csv \
  --spectrum-output power-spectrum.csv
```

```text
signal.csv
sample,value

power-spectrum.csv
frequency_bin,power
```

- Optional paths use `clap` and `PathBuf`
- `BufWriter` writes full-precision numeric CSV
- I/O failures propagate through `Result`
- Output paths must be distinct

::: notes
The files remain tool-neutral even though the repository provides a Python
helper. Participants can use their usual plotting environment instead.
:::

## Plot Both Results

```{.bash}
python3 -m pip install matplotlib

./visualize-signal-and-spectrum.py \
  signal.csv power-spectrum.csv
```

```{.bash}
./visualize-signal-and-spectrum.py \
  signal.csv power-spectrum.csv \
  --output signal-and-spectrum.png
```

- Signal: sample index against value
- Spectrum: frequency-bin index against mean-square power
- No sampling interval means no physical time or frequency units

::: notes
Use `--output` on a headless teaching system. Matplotlib selects PNG, PDF, or
SVG output from the filename extension.
:::

## Test Both Implementations

- Raw wrapper: reject invalid lengths before FFI
- Check `64 / 2 + 1 == 33`
- Detect bins 3 and 7
- Check bin powers and the mean-square identity
- Check forward/inverse errors against `1.0e-12`
- Check CSV headers and formatting
- Reject one path for both outputs

```{.bash}
cd source-code/fftw-ffi
cargo test

cd ../fftw-safe
cargo test
```

::: notes
Boundary tests protect the local raw wrapper's memory assumptions. Both
implementations retain tests for the scientific meaning and output contract.
:::

## Exercises

1. Change one frequency and predict the detected bins
2. Remove inverse normalization and explain the scale
3. Trigger a `LengthMismatch` before the native call
4. Trace cleanup after partial construction
5. Add a safe `len` method without exposing buffers
6. Compare the code owned by `fftw-ffi` and `fftw-safe`
7. Change both signals and compare their CSV output
8. Trace a query through all four `cpp-interpolation-ffi` layers

::: notes
For a short session, choose either the normalization edit or the boundary
error. Use the implementation comparison to discuss when a dependency removes
enough maintenance burden to justify its abstraction.
:::

## Module Takeaways

- FFI transfers obligations that types must recover
- Validate dimensions and conversions before native calls
- Own native memory and handles with RAII types
- Keep `unsafe` small and state its invariants
- Preserve lifetime and concurrency rules in the wrapper
- Prefer a maintained safe crate when it exposes the required native features
- Use a C facade when wrapping a C++ API directly
- Compile included native sources from `build.rs`
- Define spectral normalization before exporting results
- Keep optional visualization output outside the FFI wrapper
- Preserve units honestly in the plotting helper
- Test boundary failures and scientific behavior

::: notes
Close with the integration message: Rust can be introduced as a safe component
around established HPC libraries rather than as a demand to replace them.
:::
